body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: This little theatre, which might be rendered one of the very pleasantest places of amusement in the metropolis, if the Proprietors could but agree and would only find means of making their lobbies a little decent, has opened for the season. The company is not so good as on some former occasions, but is pretty well prepared for farce, and possesses Munden, Mathews, and Jones, from the winter theatres; Mrs. Glover also appears to be re-engaged; and Mrs. Gibbs is always useful and pleasing, sometimes even striking, as in the lively interlude of a Day after the Marriage, the moral of which is so excellent. Elliston’s loss however will be severely felt in the heroes of comedy, and Liston’s as much so perhaps in certain characters of farce which he had almost made a part of himself. The rest of the persons regularly engaged are of the old description,—gentlemen and ladies who can get no such rank at the Lyceum or Covent Garden, and who, by appearing at a theatre which is actually in the metropolis, are qualified to go down to the country at all other seasons of the year and astonish the natives with a visitation “from London,”—a phrase which is an equal recommendation all over England to bad players and bitter porter.

But there is no theatre like the one before us for new Performers. At the commencement of the season they appear in such rapid succession as almost to take away one’s breath; and every night gives one a glimpse of some face which is seldom or never perhaps to be seen again: “Come like shadows, so depart.” There is nothing to be disapproved in this system: on the contrary, its principle is a good one, inasmuch as it offers a trial of their powers to all the profession without favour or exception; but there must surely be something like a previous knowledge of the figure about to be cut by the new performer, and if so, it is hardly fair upon the public to let loose upon them such candidates for applause as the one that appeared the first night in the character of Apollo Belut. Not a joke was there about him except in the cut of his hair; and not a smile took place on the face of the audience:—a sad way of making us forget Mr. Liston! The reader will not expect observations upon actors like these, or upon a crowd of others, that either may not appear again or may sink into a level to which criticism rarely descends. At any rate, it will be sufficient to notice at present a couple of performers, who bid fair to establish themselves at this theatre,—a Mrs. Williams from Dublin, and a Mr. Grant who appeared a few months ago at Covent Garden in the character of Sir Pertinax Mac Sycophant. Mrs. Williams is in the sprightliest line of acting, romps, shewy chambermaids, &c. and occasionally reminds one of that excellent performer Miss Duncan both in voice and face:—her face is perhaps more pleasing of itself and has a much better eye; but it is not so striking, as a stage face; neither is her voice so powerful; and her person is much inferior. Her principal performance hitherto has been Peggy in the Country Girl; and notwithstanding the dangerous comparison which this part provokes with Mrs. Jordan, —a comparison which must inevitably set all actresses who have not a great genius for comedy at an immeasurable distance from her,—yet Mrs. Williams performed it with a nature and a vivacity that announced a comic feeling of no mean description. She does not manage like Mrs. Jordan, —and who does?—those thousand shadows and tones of feeling, which render her sensibility and her humour equally striking; but in the display of pure animal spirits, of an impatience at restraint, of the relish of novelty and frolic, and an incapability of containing her delight, she is not exceeded perhaps by any body;—her fingers and her restless limbs speak for her when her tongue is prevented, and the scene where she writes the two letters and deceives her guardian could hardly be performed better by Mrs. Jordan herself. In characters like these, and others of a joyous description, Mrs. Williams is a considerable acquisition to the Haymarket. She sings a little, but feebly and not in strict tune; and it is impossible not to observe, by-the-bye, the extreme deficiency of this theatre with regard to female singers. Miss Bellchambers, who has been engaged for some time, is a modest performer, and one of whom a critic would wish to speak well; but her voice is either low and poor, or loud and ill-toned; and a Mrs. Atkins, who has just arrived, and who is said to be the same Mrs. Atkins that was formerly a singer at the winter theatres, seems to make a point of differing with the orchestra to shew her contempt of their accompaniments. The performances of Mr. Grant do not excite so much comment or praise, as might have been expected from his Sir Pertinax Mac Sycophant. He seems engaged to perform sneaking Scotchmen and robustious elderly gentlemen,—and of these two different classes, is seen to much more advantage in the former. His Donald in the vulgar interlude of the Register-Office, was a good caricature of a staid, calculating, fawning rogue of a Caledonian with his beggarly pride,—such as the worst part of our northern neighbours appear, when dishonesty forces them to quit their own country and to come and scandalize it in our’s. The look which he occasionally glanced at the person whose good offices he was seeking, in order to discover whether he apprehended his right character or not, was full of meaning and such as betrays the hypocritical in spite of themselves. When he gives up his Scotch however, he appears to lose his good acting. He is never feeble, or what is called unrespectable: he appears to be too sensible a man, and to understand his author too well, for the meaner faults of the stage; but his strength is too indiscriminate; his voice is too loud, his actions too vehement and abrupt. Thus he positively converted the part of Moody in the Country Girl, who is only a violent temper and ill-bred, into that of a tragedy tyrant, with his eyes rolling about and a pompous bridling of demeanour totally out of the character. This is an exuberance, and may be mended. Let Mr. Grant take the book in his hand, and compare it honestly with the figure he acts in his looking-glass.

The new farce, How to die for Love, originally appeared on a benefit night the week before last, and succeeded so well, that it has been repeated every evening since with considerable applause. It was said at first to be the production of a German Gentleman, who had before written for the stage; but from certain epistolary documents in the Morning Chronicle, the town has been given to understand, that a German young Gentleman of fifteen translated it in the first instance from the German of Kotzebue, and that another Gentleman, also German, undertook to prepare it for the stage. Without controverting this multitude of German facts, the truth appears to be, that it is a polycheirous or multimanous production, such as Briareus might have written of old, if he had chanced to be in good humour, and to have nothing upon his hundred hands to employ him;—in plain terms, it is the work of divers persons,—a circumstance not uncommon in dramatic history, and least so at a time when every body, man, woman, and child, translates from German and French, sometimes without understanding either, and generally, whether foreigners or natives, with a perfect ignorance of the language into which they translate. An Englishman, for instance, will translate from Kotzebue, and after getting a German to correct the performance, will have it perfected for the stage by the actors; a German, or as in the instance before us, two Germans proceed vice versa, with the same histrionic finish; and with the help of a song or two or a scene from some good-natured, informing Gentleman through whose hands it passes, the piece makes its appearance as if nothing had happened,—an absolute conspiracy to make us laugh.

The style of the present farce, from its easy, idiomatic run, is evidently supplied by English hands; and the phraseology, in general, is of a more well-bred and intelligent description than is customary in modern dramas. For the rest of its merits, which are those of incident, it appears entirely indebted to its original; and so it does for its faults, which are those of sentiment, and of no ordinary description. Two German officers, Blumenfeld and Thalwick (Wrench and De Camp) are in love with the same lady, Miss Altorf (Miss Kelly) who has little or no predilection in favour of either, but is content to be married to one of them, provided they can settle the matter between themselves. Accordingly, at the suggestion of her father, who is heartily tired of the courtship and wishes to see it concluded one way or another, they agree that he who can first contrive to get the other beyond the boundary of the old gentleman's estate, shall be the happy man; and the lovers set heartily about their object, commencing operations by bribing each other's servant into their respective interests. The stratagems that result from this agreement are six in number. The first is played off in a letter to Thalwick, informing him that his mother is on her death-bed, when the fact is, that she has been dead these ten years;—the second endeavours to alarm Blumenfeld, who has a horror of infectious diseases, with an account of a plague in the village, but he detects it on the spot;—the third retorts on Thalwick with a fire, but he has unfortunately gained the secret beforehand from the brickmaker who let his shed for the purpose;—the fourth brings sudden intelligence to Blumenfeld of the rape of his mistress by Thalwick, Blumenfeld's servant pretending that he saw her carried off, and urging his master to follow; but the lady herself is in the room at the very moment, and to the dismay of the rogue comes forward at the conclusion of his story;—the fifth is Blumenfeld's final stroke: he pretends he has received a letter from his first love, which decides him on withdrawing from the contest, and all that he asks of his rival is to accompany him in a coach beyond the boundary; Thalwick consents, and Blumenfeld sends his emissary to the rendezvous, drest up to personate him and muffled up to the chin in his military cloak; the other, however, suspecting all is not right, has made the same use of his emissary, and the two officers, advancing together on the stage without seeing each other, after watching the departure of the vehicle and breaking out into triumphal exclamations, resolve at the same instant to communicate the event to their mistress, and turning about for that purpose, encounter each other full butt;—the sixth and last stratagem, with due alternation, is Thalwick's: the preceding trick enables him to pick a pretended quarrel with Blumenfeld; he forces him into a duel, insists upon receiving his shot, falls to the earth like a dying man, and succeeds in persuading the horror-stricken dupe to seek his safety in flight: the lady and her father issue out in terror upon the spot, when upon an exclamation from the old gentleman that Blumenfeld is galloping over the boundary, the deceased jumps up with a shout of victory and obtains the prize.

The Reader may easily judge of the amusing effect which some of these incidents produce in the representation. The stratagem of the plague is well put; that of the fire is droll, from its previous detection; the carrying off is better; and the disguises are excellent. But there can be no hesitation in saying, that the first and last trick, the account of the dying mother and the pretended fall in a duel, are quite unfit for sport, and absolutely unfeeling. In this respect, the piece before us, considering from whom it comes, may be regarded as a curiosity. It is a complete proof of the non-entity of all that excessive sensibility to which the German Drama lays claim, and of which Kotzebue has ever been the most obstreperous organ. To judge by the maudlin cry which this writer keeps up in his serious pieces, by the tears which he has always at hand, and the eternal white-handkerchiefs with which he supplies all his favourite characters, it might be supposed that he was the last person in the world to make a jest of anything really touching. Not he. The fact is, that to these luxurious grievers, the pathetic is only a stimulant, that delights their taste in proportion to its real callousness: it is like mustard to a palate that cannot taste without it, and brings tears into their eyes by the same rule: otherwise it is impossible that a person who feels deeply should extract farcical merriment from the innermost griefs of our nature, from filial anguish, and the despair of a man who has slain his friend. Real sensibility may occasionally put on a mask of indifference, or even merriment; but it is only for the sake of momentary contrast and relief: it is only an impatience that hurries into extremes for a new sensation,—a sort of convulsion, by which the burden endeavours to throw itself off; but no man, who felt the charities of the heart profoundly, as Kotzebue pretends to do, would ever think of making a dying mother and a distracted friend subservient to the purposes of stage drollery. It might be argued, that the mother is not dead, the friend has no reason to be distracted, and therefore we need not take it in an unfeeling light, but it might as well be argued for a tragedy, that one person is not dead, and another is not distracted, and therefore we should not take it in a feeling light. The sentiment of the thing is unseasonably and unwarrantably brought forward, and that is enough: our best feelings are torn up by the roots to tickle our faces with. Indeed, the whole conduct of the piece is want of feeling and delicacy throughout. A young lady consents to be married to one of two men upon the mere toss of a halfpenny; the two men both think her an angel notwithstanding, and what is still worse for lovers, are willing to let each other have such a chance; they then begin playing off such stratagems as would disgust any woman of feeling; and in fine, the one who loses the game, returns to enjoy the other's success by way of being generous, and vows that he will be the merriest man of the party. So much for German sensibility and the moral tact.—Let us enjoy Mr. Kotzebue's farces as much as we please; but considering his notions of what the farcial is, let us in common justice consider his serious dramas in the same light, and regard his feeling as a farce also.
